questions.problem: Which of the following is the graph of the polar curve  $\theta =\frac{11\pi }{10}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The polar curve defined by the equation $\theta =\frac{11\pi }{10}$ is the ray that starts at the origin and makes a counterclockwise angle of $\frac{11\pi }{10}$ with the positive $x$-axis. 

Therefore, the angle it makes with the negative $x$-axis is 

$$
\frac{11\pi }{10}-\pi =\frac{\pi }{10}.
$$

 

The correct answer is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13980294/assets/802bb767b28c38598663d928d66338086adf08b80bc5887a7795704183ed2212.png)

Given that the ray above passes through the point with Cartesian coordinates $(4,5)$, find the polar equation of the ray.
questions.worked_solution:
The angles that the ray makes with the positive $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{5}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since the ray lies in the first quadrant, its polar equation is

$$
\theta =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{5}{4}).
$$

Given that the ray above passes through the point with Cartesian coordinates $(-\sqrt{6},-\sqrt{2})$, find the polar equation of the ray.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the reference angle associated with the point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{R} & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{y}{x}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡|\frac{-\sqrt{2}}{-\sqrt{6}}| \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the ray lies in the third quadrant. So, we find the angle in the third quadrant that has a reference angle ${\theta }_{R}=\frac{\pi }{6},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\theta  & =\pi +{\theta }_{R} \\  & =\pi +\frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{7\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the polar equation of the ray is 

$$
\theta =\frac{7\pi }{6}.
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13980294/assets/5e29d99fc6ae3a848bfe59ab9e77595ab9ca2a605d0d03139e8599adf15e6fd9.png)

The polar curve $r=9$ and the ray $\theta =\frac{3\pi }{4}$ intersect at the point $P,$ as shown above. The Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are$\,(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
questions.worked_solution:
The polar coordinates of $P$ are $(r,\theta )=(9,\frac{3\pi }{4}).$ We can convert the polar coordinates of $P$ to Cartesian coordinates, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =9cos\,(\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\  & =9\cdot -\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =-\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =9sin\,(\frac{3\pi }{4}) \\  & =9\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(-\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{2},\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{2}).$
